segments.title: Source reliability and why citations matter
segments.body: Choosing sources is a practical research skill. The Terry Pratchett example shows that a source can be excellent for one question and unsuitable for another, so authority must be judged against the subject being investigated. Citations reveal both the tools a student used and whether the work moved beyond the assigned reading list into independent research. Evaluating evidence this way provides a foundation for an academic or historical argument.

evidence.note: A critical literature review needs an appropriate amount of relevant information from sources whose reliability fits the research question.
The Terry Pratchett example contrasts a source useful within its fictional subject with one unsuitable for real-world engineering history.
References show which tools the student used and whether independent research is taking place.

segments.summary: Relevance, reliability, and visible citations distinguish usable research from an attractive but unsuitable source.

segments.title: Presentation polish affects how work is read
segments.body: In the studies cited here, professionally aligned versions of the same work received slightly higher marks. The explanation offered is ordinary marker psychology: neat structure encourages a reader to look for credit, while clutter and weak paragraphing make omissions more conspicuous. Formatting cannot replace evidence or analysis. It can make substantive work easier to read and reward.

evidence.note: Studies of marking found slightly higher scores for professionally aligned presentation even when the underlying content was identical.
The positive reading encouraged by a neat paper compared with the fault-finding response invited by untidy structure.

segments.summary: A practical aside explains why tidy alignment and paragraph structure can shape a marker's first response even when the underlying content is unchanged.

segments.title: Read prose aloud to expose weak style
segments.body: Read a draft aloud to check its wording. Silent reading tends to supply the wording the writer intended, which can conceal clumsy or broken prose. Hearing the sentences makes those faults much harder to overlook. Before submission, this tests whether an argument reads as clearly as it seemed while drafting.

evidence.note: Silent reading can supply the wording a writer intended, whereas reading aloud exposes language that actually sounds wrong.

segments.summary: Reading a draft aloud reveals awkward phrasing that silent reading often repairs unconsciously.

segments.title: Ethics can require more than best practice
segments.body: Best practice is the accepted correct procedure; ethics concerns the judgment about what is right. The two should ordinarily support each other. When accepted practice goes astray, the researcher still has to decide whether following it is ethically defensible. Following an accepted method does not remove personal responsibility.

evidence.note: The transcript defines ethics and best practice separately, says they should align, and advises choosing the ethically correct course when practice goes astray.

segments.summary: A short caution separates accepted best practice from the ethically right action when procedure and judgment no longer align.

segments.title: Use corroboration to find consensus and outliers
segments.body: Corroboration requires active comparison among multiple sources on similar subjects and from similar periods. Agreement supplies a defensible consensus and several references for the same point. Outliers may contribute information that the majority view misses, so disagreement deserves attention too. Critical history writing establishes what sources share, then explains where and why they diverge.

evidence.note: The transcript recommends comparing several books and continuing to seek modern works and journal articles.
How agreement creates a consensus view and disagreement identifies outliers that support critical analysis.

segments.summary: Comparing several books and journal articles helps establish a consensus view while preserving dissenting sources for critical analysis.

segments.title: A polished answer still has to answer the question
segments.body: A beautifully written and thoroughly researched essay can still earn a poor mark if it does not answer the assigned question. The mistake is compared to a carpenter delivering six fine rocking chairs when a client ordered a dining table and chairs. Craft quality does not compensate for producing the wrong object. Check relevance before investing further effort in research.

evidence.note: The transcript warns that strong writing and research cannot compensate for answering a question different from the assignment.
Comparison of the error to delivering six rocking chairs when a six-seat dining table was requested.

segments.summary: The rocking-chair analogy shows why excellent research and prose cannot rescue an essay that answers a question the student invented.

segments.title: Build research from a rough plan and a key text
segments.body: Planning begins before extensive source collection. Start with a rough plan and a key text, consulting a subject librarian or module guide to locate appropriate material. Those first discoveries should improve the plan before the researcher gathers more sources. This sequence keeps reading tied to the assignment and involves the subject librarian early in the research.

evidence.note: The transcript recommends a rough plan, a key text, and help from the subject librarian or module guide.
The key text and rough plan should produce a better plan before more sources are gathered.

segments.summary: Draft a rough plan, consult a key text and subject librarian, then gather further sources around a better plan.

segments.title: Balance research evidence with analysis
segments.body: Too little information produces waffle, while indiscriminate collection produces a list of facts without an argument. A typical marking scheme may offer two or three analysis marks for every mark attached to evidence. A 3,000-word essay dominated by 2,500 words of new information therefore leaves too little room to earn the analysis marks. Writers need to budget space for interpretation and critical thinking as well as research findings.

evidence.note: Insufficient research produces waffle, while an essay overloaded with facts leaves too little space for the analysis the assignment requires.
A rough evidence-to-analysis marking ratio applied to a 3,000-word assignment's word budget.

segments.summary: The marking example explains why both under-research and fact-heavy writing fail when the assignment rewards analysis more heavily than evidence alone.

segments.title: Use SEAL to keep paragraphs analytical and relevant
segments.body: SEAL gives an academic paragraph a structure: statement, evidence, analysis, and link. Test how the evidence relates both to the argument and to the assigned question. One paragraph where those relationships differ may contain productive thought, but several in succession signal that the essay has wandered away from its task. The final link should carry the reader into the next paragraph so the report or essay holds together as a continuous argument.

evidence.note: The transcript defines SEAL and asks how the evidence relates separately to the writer's argument and the assigned question.
Consecutive paragraphs whose evidence relates differently to the argument and question can signal an essay drifting off topic.
The passage returns to signposting, evidence, analysis, and links that make the whole essay flow.

segments.summary: SEAL structures an academic paragraph as statement, evidence, analysis, and link while testing whether each point serves both the argument and the question.

segments.title: What a critical literature review demonstrates
segments.body: A critical literature review makes several research abilities visible. Broad reading helps a researcher understand the topic and locate the new work within existing knowledge. The finished review must also show that the writer can hold and compare several sources at once. Because markers can reward only what appears on the page, those comparisons and critical analysis must be expressed explicitly.

evidence.note: The transcript defines the review as evidence of broad understanding, engagement with multiple sources, and critical analysis.
Comparison of multiple pieces of information must appear on the page before it can earn marks.

segments.summary: A critical literature review demonstrates broad understanding, simultaneous consideration of multiple sources, and visible critical thinking.

segments.title: A starter formula for organizing the review
segments.body: This formula provides a starting point that writers can adapt. For a roughly 3,000-word review, identify key areas and find a reputable journal article, textbook, and web article for each, adjusting the number of areas to the assignment length. Each section begins with the journal article, compares it with the textbook, contrasts both with the web source, and summarizes their relationship to the broader question. Repeating that pattern keeps different authors, publication years, and source types in comparison while the writer develops an individual style.

evidence.note: The transcript begins with a core text, turns the topic into key areas, and scales their number to the assignment length.
A reputable journal article, textbook, and web article for each area, with a subject librarian helping check uncertain web material.
The section gives the compare-and-contrast order for each area and presents it as a simple starting point from which writers develop their own style.

segments.summary: The starter method divides the topic into key areas and compares a journal article, textbook, and web article within each section.

segments.title: Compare source types by reliability and currency
segments.body: The three source types provide useful tension because they undergo different checks. A reputable journal article tends to carry the strongest academic checking through peer review, though journal standards vary. A textbook has usually passed editing and library or departmental selection, giving it a measure of stability. A web article may contain the newest and most provocative information, but it has often received the fewest checks and therefore demands the most careful reliability assessment.

evidence.note: Journal articles tend to be the most academically reliable because of peer review, though journals differ in quality.
Editing and selection by libraries or academic departments give textbooks a measure of stability as research sources.
Web articles are described as potentially the newest and most interesting sources but also the least checked and possibly least reliable.

segments.summary: Journal articles, textbooks, and web articles carry different balances of peer review, editorial stability, novelty, and risk.
